quote: the electric company went crazy. They sent me a $2,300.
stewart_read: This is the single richest anchor the customer handed the rep on the whole call — a specific dollar figure delivered with visible frustration ('went crazy'). The rep's very next line is a logistics question about which trees are cut down, meaning the bill was never even acknowledged, let alone flipped into 'that's exactly the amount solar would eliminate.'
alternative_hypothesis: The rep could have been deliberately staying focused on the roof-photo logistics as the more urgent blocker before circling back to the bill later in the call — but no such circle-back ever happens, so this reads as a miss rather than a sequencing choice.
coaching_implication: Replay this exact moment with the rep — when a customer hands over a bill number unprompted, it needs an immediate acknowledgment ('that's rough, that's exactly the kind of bill solar is built to erase') before moving to the next question.

quote: if it was looking at it now, you guys see the head topping trailer.
stewart_read: The customer is trying to describe how open his roof currently is compared to outdated satellite imagery — an opportunity to build curiosity about what the actual design would show once updated. The rep just says 'Gotcha' and asks a narrow follow-up rather than building anticipation ('once we get a current photo, you'll probably see a design that looks a lot better than what's on file').
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may have been intentionally holding back detail to avoid setter scope creep on design specifics — a defensible restraint. But the miss here is about creating forward-pull, not about explaining panel mechanics, so scope discipline doesn't excuse the flat response.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to mirror customer effort with anticipation-building language rather than flat acknowledgments — cheap, low-risk, and keeps momentum.

quote: I've got two trees that can handle the, hail. And I'm not trying to I'll take these both of them down.
stewart_read: The customer is volunteering ongoing, self-motivated site prep (tree removal) specifically to make his roof more solar-viable — a strong signal of intent and initiative that most leads never offer unprompted. The rep's response is a flat 'Okay. Gotcha.'
coaching_implication: This is exactly the kind of unsolicited operational detail that should be reflected back ('that's great, that'll really open things up for the design') to reward and reinforce the customer's own momentum — a free rapport-and-motivation builder the rep let pass.

quote: Okay. What I could do is I could get started on things on our end. I'll send you a quick text to if you wouldn't wouldn't mind if you have time later today to send me a photo just of kind of the back of your roof.
stewart_read: This is a reasonable ad hoc workaround for the outdated satellite imagery problem — asking for a current roof photo makes sense given the design blocker the customer raised. But it is not a substitute for locking an appointment; the rep treats sending the photo as the entire next step rather than pairing it with a specific date/time for the design review call.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: the rep may be sequencing correctly — get the photo first, then book — since a design genuinely can't be built without current roof visibility. But even so, the rep never returns to lock a day/time once the photo plan is agreed, so the call still ends without appointment mechanics.
coaching_implication: Even when a legitimate blocker (bad imagery) requires an extra step, the rep should still anchor a specific callback day/time ('I'll call you tomorrow at 5 once I have your photo') rather than leaving it as 'we'll figure out a good time.'

quote: Gotcha. Okay. Yeah. Well, just send me a photo when you can. We'll start on our end, and then we can kinda figure out a time over text. Would that work for you?
stewart_read: This is the call's closing line and it contains no date, no time, no hour-block, no 'is that fair' handshake — just a vague plan to 'figure out a time over text.' Per button_up requirements, none of the required elements (datetime, one-hour block, no-driving/computer instruction, handshake) are present.
alternative_hypothesis: Given the customer's rambling, fatigued state by this point ('I'm tired'), the rep may have judged that pushing for a hard time slot risked friction — a defensible read-the-room call. But the schema still requires the rep to circle back later with specifics, and there's no evidence a text-based day/time follow-up plan was actually detailed here.
coaching_implication: Coach button-up discipline: even a soft, low-pressure close should still name a concrete next contact point ('I'll text you tonight and we'll lock in Thursday or Friday') rather than leaving the appointment fully open-ended.

quote: Hey, Johnny. This is Parker with Ion.
stewart_read: The intro states the rep's name and company but omits any state reference, lead-source framing, or Tesla-certified language that the script's legitimacy-first design calls for. Combined with a talk-over moment right after ('What was that? Sorry.' at 00:21), the open is generic rather than a clean legitimacy anchor.
alternative_hypothesis: The customer's immediate enthusiasm ('hoping y'all come and put it in') suggests legitimacy was not actually in question on this particular call, so the omission may not have cost anything here.
coaching_implication: Still worth flagging as a habit check — a stronger intro (referencing the form/request source explicitly, pausing cleanly) costs nothing and protects the rep on calls where the customer isn't already this receptive.
